newsitem.title: UK: UK markets foresee third rate rise in three months.
newsitem.headline: UK markets foresee third rate rise in three months.

text.p: British financial markets were holding their breath on Thursday morning, awaiting news from the Bank of England, due at 1100 GMT, on whether the UK faces its third rise in official interest rates in as many months.

Official interest rates are expected to rise to 6.75 percent from 6.5 but dealers say there is an outside chance of a more stringent half-point increase as the central bank struggles to calm the exuberant consumer sector.
"The budget forecast that we would miss the inflation target and that gave the Bank the green light to raise interest rates," SBC-Warburg UK economist Darren Winder said.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown empowered the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee to set interest rates in May and analysts believe the absence of budget measures to stifle consumer demand leaves the onus on the Bank to use interest rates to prevent a surge in inflation.
"I didn't think the budget would do enough to prevent further rate rises but it did even less than I expected," Winder said.

Brown disappointed financial markets with a tax increased of 5.5 billion stg aimed largely at the corporate sector, leaving consumers free to continue their spending spree, financed by windfall payments totalling 30 billion stg from building society mergers and flotations.
The UK government bond market retraced some of Wednesday's losses in early trade but remained extremely nervous. The LIFFE gilt contract was 1/32 higher at 114-10/32.

The equity market recorded slight losses after an overnight slump in U.S. shares and amid caution over the outcome of the monetary meeting. The Financial Times-Stock Exchange 100-share index fell 17.4 points to 4745.0.

Whilst on the foreign exchanges, which have seen the most fevered speculation about interest rates, traders had already placed their bets and the pound was barely moved at 2.9680/90 marks and $1.6835/42 compared with 2.9671/81 and $1.6844/49 in late European trading on Wednesday.

Dealers say the unit is poised to tackle 3.0 marks if the Bank does raise interest rates, in what would undoubtedly be another blow for Britain's hard-pressed exporters, already reeling from the impact of the pound's 20 percent rise in less than a year.

"The impact on sterling is one of the main reasons we don't expect a half-point rise. We've already seen data showing manufacturing output fell more than one percent in May," HSBC economist Dharshini David said.
"We're saying we could even be looking at 3.10 marks by the end of third quarter, in which case manufacturing is going to be hammered," she said.

The Bank of England has expressed concern about the sharp contrast between the buoyant consumer and service sectors and the sluggish manufacturing sector but analysts believe the needs of manufacturers will have to be sacrificed to the wider demands of making sure the UK economy does not end up with another unsustainable boom.

"While the economy is experiencing these windfalls it is better to err on the side of having too tight a monetary stance rather than too loose, that means higher interest rates and a strong pound," SBC's Winder said.
Dealers say that the worst possible outcome for the market's is no rate rise at all because this would lead to speculation that the Bank had left it too late to prevent a build-up in inflation.
But Royal Bank of Scotland economist Neil Parker is amongst the few dissenters who are predicting that rates will remain unchanged.
"We forecast the Bank of England to leave rates on hold and take more time to assess data relating to a period after the previous rate hikes," he said.
Brown raised interest rates by 25 basis points in May before ceding control of rates to the central bank and the Bank itself increased rates by 25 basis points last month.
--Cheryl Juckes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
The 1/4 point increase had been widely predicted by bank economists after last week's first budget by the new Labour government was seen as being not sufficiently tough to rein in consumer demand.
Speculation gathered pace after the government released data this week showing that the underlying inflation rate had shot above the government's 2.5 percent target to stand at 2.7 percent for June.

In a statement released after the announcement from the Bank, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said it was important that inflation be brought under control to avoid a return to boom and bust cycles of the past.
After the rate rise sterling dropped over one pfennig against the German mark as traders on the foreign exchange markets had been expecting an even stronger increase of 1/2 point.
